keys.why: What this course calls the folder holding one page per curriculum expectation. Declared by every payload and skeleton manifest and carried here at creation; the build tries it FIRST and only then falls back to scanning for a top-level folder whose name contains 'curriculum'. The fallback is still the real path for a course made from scratch, which has no manifest to declare anything — but a course whose folder is called something else entirely would otherwise never have its map built at all.

Which per-section folder holds this course's class pages. ABSENT or unmatched falls back to the old GUESS — the first per-section folder whose name contains 'class' (case-insensitive), else the first entry, else the literal 'All Classes' — which is what every course made before this key existed relies on. The key exists because the guess quietly decided what a teacher was allowed to CALL this folder: somebody whose vocabulary is 'Thread 2, Day 3' would sensibly call it 'All Days', and under the guess alone that folder is not found, so the first per-section folder is used instead and the curriculum map counts the wrong pages. The map does not FAIL when that happens — it falls back to counting every published page, which is a wrong map that reports success. Written by both wizards at creation, and MATERIALISED by a rename: renaming the class folder writes this key even on a course that never had one, because a rename is the one moment Plantoir witnesses the change. Compared case-insensitively, and the LIST's spelling wins over the key's, because everything downstream builds file paths from the answer. A club (#267) records “All Meetings” here, which does not say 'class' — so the recorded name is the only thing that finds its pages, and a course setup re-run must pass the recorded name in rather than re-guess.

What this course calls the first half of a class page's name — “Unit 2, Day 3”, or “Module 2, Day 3”. ABSENT means “Unit”, which is what every course made before this key existed says; empty means the same, and the two are deliberately NOT distinguished the way graded_folders distinguishes them, because there is no sensible reading of “the teacher cleared the word” and a course whose class pages had no name could not be built. Until 2026-09-01 the word was a structural assumption rather than a preference: the regex deciding whether a page is a class page, the page the next-class button writes, and the curriculum map's idea of what a course TEACHES all had it built in — so a teacher who renamed the pages in Obsidian lost every feature that recognises a class page, and the coverage map does not FAIL when it finds none, it falls back to counting every published page, which is a wrong map that reports success. Chosen at course creation, where the ready-made pages are poured in the teacher's word rather than renamed afterwards — and, since 2026-09-10, changeable on a course ALREADY IN USE from the app's Course Settings, which renames every class page in every section, retitles it and rewrites every wikilink pointing at it, across shared folders too, with a backup first and a record of a rename under way so an interrupted one is finished rather than left half done. That was the far more dangerous half — not because of scale (a ready-made course holds 84–87 class pages — 42 for the two half-credit courses, CHV2O and GLC2O; the 3,172 figure quoted elsewhere is the total across all 38 payloads), but because a half-finished pass leaves a broken site with no way back; the rules are class-planning.json → renamingTheUnitWord and the sentences shared-rules.json → specialNames.renameUnitWord. The build needs no change for it: it reads the word from this file on every run. “Day” is deliberately not configurable — a teacher who says “Thread” almost certainly still says “Day 3”. Under `class_page_scheme: "numbered"` the same key is the whole word of a ONE-number name — a club writes “Week”, so its pages are “Week 3” — reused deliberately rather than joined by a second word key, so the key's name now under-describes it. A numbered course's word is chosen when the course is made and is not renamed afterwards.

The SHAPE of this course's class-page names (#267). "unit_day" is “<unit_word> 2, Day 3”; "numbered" is “<unit_word> 3”, one number counting meetings — what a club writes. ABSENT means "unit_day", and so does any value a reader does not know: a scheme a newer app wrote, opened by an older one, reads as today's shape (it then sees no class pages — degraded, never corrupting) and nothing is rewritten. Written by the new-course wizard for a CLUB only (with front_page_heading and class_noun) — every other course's file stays byte-for-byte what it was, which absence already describes — chosen there and NOT switchable afterwards: Course Settings shows it locked. A course made before the key existed (Russell's CODING, whose pages are already “Week N”) can never become numbered by opening it.

The heading each section's front page is created with, above the embed of the newest class (#267): a club writes “Most Recent Meeting”. ABSENT means “Most Recent Class” for a course being created — but for a course that already exists it means only that nothing was recorded: its pages say whatever they say (CODING's reads “Most Recent Meeting”), so Course Settings shows the absent key as not recorded, never as this default (shared-rules.json → wizard.clubToggle.settingsRows.frontPageHeadingNotSet). Read ONLY when a course is created — the course setup writes it into a new numbered course's front pages — and never by whatever repoints the front page, which finds the embed by the class page it names, not by the heading; a teacher's own heading is therefore never fought over. Not switchable after the wizard; Course Settings shows it locked.

What the assistant calls one of this course's class pages when it talks to the teacher (#267): a club writes "meeting". ABSENT means "class", and so does any unknown value. A closed pair rather than free text because the sentences carry articles and plurals (“a meeting”, “meetings”); each variant is written out in full in the app's wording. Read by both apps only — the build never reads it — and it moves no byte of what the assistant's model is shown. Not switchable after the wizard; Course Settings shows it locked.

Folder names whose contents count for marks — what makes an expectation 'assessed' on the Curriculum Coverage map. ABSENT (not `[]`) for every course that has not been asked, and that distinction is load-bearing: absent means the historical rule applies (any folder whose name contains 'task'), while `[]` means the teacher deliberately cleared the list. Seeding an existing course with ["Tasks"] would silently drop folders the old substring rule counted, such as the skeletons' "Thinking Tasks". See shared-rules.json -> gradedFolders.

Extra destinations a course ALSO publishes to, beyond `deploy_target` (the primary) — for redundancy against one host having a bad day. `type` uses the same spellings as `deploy_target`; `path` is only present for `local_folder` entries. ABSENT (not `[]`) for every course that has not opted in, so a course nobody has touched writes the exact same file it always has.

keys.type: object with keys 'shared' (array of strings) and/or 'per_section' (array of strings)
keys.why: Names of folders or files excluded from previews and deploys, separated by scope. Keyed by scope ('shared' and/or 'per_section') to match the config's structure. Course-wide within a scope. ABSENT (not `{}`) when nothing is excluded.

keys.type: per-section map of (per-destination-type map of strings), e.g. custom_domains.sections.section1.netlify
keys.why: Keyed by destination TYPE (`netlify`, `cloudflare_pages` — never `local_folder`, which has no domain concept), not just by section, because a course can publish to more than one destination at once and a domain meant for one must never be applied to another's own link. An OLDER shape — `custom_domains.sections.sectionN` as a bare string, written before a course could have more than one destination — is still read: as the domain for whichever destination is currently `deploy_target` (the primary), and invisible to every other type. Setting a domain for a second destination migrates a bare string it finds into the new shape rather than discarding it.
EMPTY means Netlify, and that is not an oversight: every course written before the other destinations existed has no key at all, and must keep working.

How late a deploy set to happen on its own may still go ahead. ABSENT means 7, and so does anything that is not one of the values above — an older build's number, a value hand-edited into the file — because the alternative is honouring a stored 0 and standing every scheduled deploy down. Written by the settings form and by nothing else; the wizard deliberately does not ask, since a course that has never been deployed cannot be scheduled at all. READ AT THE MOMENT THE DEPLOY FIRES, out of this file, by a process with no app around it — so changing it after scheduling changes what a job already set will do. The rule it feeds, and what was rejected, is shared-rules.json → scheduledDeployCancellation. Added on the mac 2026-09-20; the Python does not read it and does not need to, and neither does a build.

Whether clicking a folder in the site's explorer expands it rather than navigating. Read by `setup_course.py` and baked into Explorer.tsx by `build_site.py` — so this is a key the PYTHON acts on, and an app that never writes it leaves the teacher's choice unrecorded. Found missing from this contract by the count check on its first run, which is what that check is for.

Folders and files kept out of the built site's sidebar (they are still built, linkable and searchable). Written by the setup wizard and the apps ONLY: since issue #265 (2026-09-24) the build never changes it, where it used to take a folder it thought new back out and write the list back. See sidebarHiding.
The timetable sections a teacher actually teaches — not 1...N. A teacher with sections 2 and 5 has exactly those.
Absent means TRUE — the 'S1' marker shows unless a teacher turns it off.

TRUE marks a REFERENCE COURSE: last year's course, or a course full of example content, kept in this year's sidebar to be read and never deployed. ABSENT MEANS FALSE, which is what every course written before this key existed says, and it is the only safe direction — a course that forgot to say it is ordinary is one a teacher can still deploy, while the reverse would make a live course silently undeployable. The marker is NOT the defence on its own, and that is the part worth carrying: a reference course is ALSO left with nowhere to deploy to (deploy_target 'local_folder' with an empty deploy_folder_path, no additional_deploy_targets, no custom_domains, and its .netlify_sites/.cloudflare_sites markers renamed aside), so an OLDER copy of either app sharing the same folder over iCloud Drive — one that has never heard of this key — refuses the deploy too, in sentences it already ships. Measured on a real previous-generation working folder: those configs carry no deploy_target at all, and an absent deploy_target reads as 'netlify', so a plain copy really would arrive with a working Deploy button aimed at last year's live class site. The refusal itself is shared-rules.json → referenceCourses.

Which school year a reference course was taught in, as the calendar year it STARTED in: 2025 means 2025–26. Only meaningful beside kept_for_reference. The LABEL is derived rather than stored — 'Other' for absent or null, otherwise SchoolYear's rule — so the en dash in '2025–26' never reaches this file and the two apps cannot render the same year two ways. Absent, null, or anything that is not a whole number within the offered range reads as 'Other', which is the safe direction: a course lands in a group the teacher can see and can change, rather than inventing a group labelled '0000–01' out of a value that coerced to zero. A year ABOVE the range today (a Mac with a wrong clock) joins its own group on the day that year arrives, because the range only ever grows at the top. Nil CLEARS the key rather than writing null, so a course nobody has filed under a year writes the same file it always did.

courseConfigKeys.note: `courses/<CODE>/course_config.json`. Written by the wizard and the settings form, read by both apps AND by `scripts/*.py` — so a key spelled differently on one platform is not a disagreement between two apps, it is a setting the site build silently ignores. Nested keys are per-section maps: `{"sections": {"section1": <value>}}`. The keys fall into TWO groups, and a first draft of this contract only had the first: the settings form round-trips most of them, while a handful are written ONCE by the wizard and read back by `setup_course.py` as the defaults for its own questions. Missing the second group means a teacher on one platform is asked a question the other platform answers for them.

rules.detail: Read the documented default and carry on.
rules.rule: An ABSENT key is not an error
rules.why: Courses created by older versions are missing keys that exist today, and they must open without complaint.

rules.detail: Read the file, change what the teacher changed, write the rest back untouched.
rules.rule: Keys a platform does not understand are PRESERVED
rules.why: The two apps ship at different times. A course saved by the newer one must not lose its settings when opened by the older, and a key dropped this way is invisible until a teacher notices their footer has gone.

keys.requirement: BOTH apps ask the teacher and write the answer. Decided 2026-08-16: Windows matches macOS.
keys.why: Whether a course that is NOT TAKING a ready-made payload starts from its subject's SKELETON — folders that suit the subject, four units of class pages to rename, placeholders saying what belongs where — or from nothing. Around 1,900 course codes have a skeleton and no payload, so this is the question most teachers actually meet; the 38 codes that DO have a payload meet it too, the moment they turn the payload down (GitHub issue #248, 2026-09-21 — before then both apps wrote false for those codes whatever the teacher chose, and the course arrived empty). Both apps write `hasSkeleton(code, takingExampleContent:) && teacherSaidYes`, and this key is never true beside `prepopulate_example_content: true` — one starting content source or neither. (Windows did not write it at all until 2026-09-07, so for three weeks the Python took its own default of TRUE and a Windows teacher could not decline.) The wizard's structure EDITOR must agree with this key in both directions — turning the toggle off puts the generic defaults back rather than leaving the skeleton's folders on screen for a course that will not have them — and that rule, with its cases, is in shared-rules.json → wizard.skeletonToggle.

Whether one of the 38 ready-made courses is poured in (counted 2026-09-22 — count the folders in support/example_content rather than trusting a number here). Written as `hasContent(code) && teacherSaidYes`, so a stale true can never mean anything.

Whether the curriculum pages written for this course code come with it — every expectation as its own page, and what the curriculum coverage map is built from. TWO starting points reach them, and this said only the first until GitHub issue #251 (2026-09-22): the teacher TAKING the payload gets its Curriculum folder, and the teacher who DECLINES the payload but keeps the subject's skeleton gets those same pages installed into the skeleton's Curriculum folder. Both apps write `curriculumPagesOffered && teacherSaidYes`, where curriculumPagesOffered is: the code has a payload, that payload declares a curriculum folder, AND either the payload is being taken or a skeleton is offered and wanted. `setup_course.py` reads this key as the answer to its own curriculum question, so an app that writes false here never runs the install branch however its interface looks — the course gets the skeleton's placeholder Curriculum folder (a generic index and one fake expectation called A1.1) and the coverage map has one fake cell to colour, with every gate on both platforms green. MEASURED: ICS4U 2 curriculum pages to 61, MCMPR11 to 59 British Columbia standards with no A1.1, ICS2O — no payload — unchanged at 2. The ~1,900 codes with no payload always write false: their skeleton ships an empty Curriculum folder, ready for expectations the teacher adds by hand.

wizardAnswerKeys.note: Written by the WIZARD at course creation, not by the settings form. `setup_course.py` reads each as the default for a question it would otherwise ask — so an app that omits one leaves the Python to take its own default, and the teacher never gets the choice. All three are the TEACHER's answers, on both platforms: the wizard asks, the app writes `capabilityExists && teacherSaidYes`, and the Python's own default is a fallback that should never be the thing deciding.

cases.why: A quoted date with a note after it (review of #199): the time and offset are read INSIDE the quotes, so the new date does not end in a stray `"` — a date Quartz cannot read and silently replaces with today. The quotes and the note go whole with the old value.

writingCases.note: GitHub #199. The date and title writers — the mac's PageFrontmatter.settingCreated (key + day; the time and offset already on the line are kept, and `T07:00:00.000-0400` is used when none can be read) and settingTitle — take a key's CONTINUATION lines with it, the rule #176 gave the visibility writer (PageVisibilityReader.continuationLineIndices / Windows' ContinuationLines): walk forward over blank lines and `# note`s, stop at the first line that is not indented, take everything to the last indented value line. `expectSiteReads` is what python-frontmatter 1.3.0 / PyYAML 6.0.3 read from `after` — the parse process_frontmatter re-dumps for Quartz — measured 2026-09-25, and checked again inside the image by scripts/check_dates_and_titles_against_the_site.py. Before the fix the same writers replaced the key's line alone: a date or title below its key, folded, or quoted over two lines read as the new value and the old one JOINED (`2026-09-24T07:00:00.000-0400 2026-09-08T07:00:00.000-0400`, `Unit 1, Day 2 Unit 1, Day 1`, `Unit 1, Day 2 Day 1"`), and a note between key and value STOPPED the build (ParserError) — while the app read the new value, so the two disagreed in silence. The same replacement is made by SectionAdder when a section's landing page is copied into a new section. Compare whole files as bytes.

firstDeployMarkers.note: How each app knows whether a section has EVER been deployed to where it is going now. `deploy.py` writes a marker the first time a section goes out, and the apps read it to decide whether a deploy would ask a question — which is what makes a scheduled deploy safe or a 06:30 failure.

paths.why: A folder deploy asks nothing, so it keeps no marker and counts as always-deployed.

releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.name: section<N>.previous-yyyy-MM-dd_HHmmss.json, beside the marker it replaces
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.legacyName: .netlify_site.previous-yyyy-MM-dd_HHmmss.json, for the older marker that deploy.py still reads and migrates back into the stable path — in the BUILT OUTPUT, never beside the teacher's pages. WHERE THE BUILT OUTPUT IS DIFFERS BY PLATFORM, and getting that wrong is the easy mistake in both directions: <CODE>/.merged_output/section<N>/ on macOS, but %LOCALAPPDATA%\Plantoir\builds\<folder id>\<CODE>\section<N>\ on Windows, because merged_output_root() returns PLANTOIR_BUILD_ROOT/<CODE> with no .merged_output level whenever that variable is set and deploy.ps1 sets it unconditionally. An app that releases only the OTHER platform's spelling releases a path that has never held a marker, so the release does nothing at all and the section goes on publishing over last year's site. Both are attempted on Windows, guarded by existence, so a folder carried across from a mac is covered too.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.rule: Cutting a section loose from last year's website RENAMES its marker aside, never deletes it, and does so for EVERY destination type rather than only the one the course is configured for now.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.why: Renamed rather than deleted because the file holds the site's id and its admin address, and a teacher who decides they wanted last year's website after all has no other way back to it. Every destination rather than the primary one because markers are keyed purely by destination TYPE and a course can carry additional targets, so releasing only the primary leaves an additional destination still overwriting last year's site. The name is frozen and shared so a teacher is told the same filename whichever app they are sitting at.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.windowsOwes: ✅ Done 2026-09-08 (GitHub issues #66 and #69, GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md row 458). Both halves are fixed and both were real: AssistWorkspace.ReleaseSite returned INSIDE the first folder that held a marker, so a section pinned to both Netlify and Cloudflare kept publishing over last year's Cloudflare site; and it did not know the legacy path. It now walks every destination in one undo transaction, returns a record that keeps "still pinned" apart from "there was nothing to release", and releases the legacy marker at BOTH spellings above. Kept in place rather than deleted, so this block reads as the history of a fixed defect rather than as an outstanding one.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.safeBecause: deploy.py and build_site.py build exact marker paths and never glob the folder, so a .previous-*.json sitting beside them is inert.

firstDeployMarkers.rule: Read the marker for the destination the course is configured for NOW — not any marker, and not the other one.
firstDeployMarkers.why: A course deployed to Netlify and then switched to Cloudflare has NEVER been deployed to Cloudflare, and its first Cloudflare deploy will ask what to call the site. Treating the old Netlify marker as proof schedules exactly the deploy that stops at a prompt at half six with nobody there — the failure the 'never been deployed' refusal exists to prevent.

note: The two files both apps WRITE, and the Python then reads. Everything else in these contracts describes behaviour; this describes a format, and a format that drifts corrupts a teacher's course quietly. Both spellings below have already caused a real bug: `SectionAdder` was found writing the OLD frontmatter key on both platforms, so a section added through the app was born in a schema everything else had moved off, and the TEST agreed with the code.

pageVisibility.note: Frontmatter. Whether students see a page — the single most consequential field in the product, since getting it backwards publishes something a teacher held back. TWO spellings exist and both must be read: `publish:` (current) and `draft:` (legacy, meaning the OPPOSITE). Course-level pages carry a key per section instead. THE ANSWER IS THE BUILT SITE'S ANSWER, and that is not the same as reading the line: `build_site.process_frontmatter` loads every page with python-frontmatter (PyYAML, YAML 1.1), resolves the per-section keys onto a plain `publish:` and writes it back, and Quartz then parses THAT with js-yaml on its JSON schema before `patches/publish.ts` drops a page whose flag is the boolean false or the exact string "false". So `publish: no` hides a page, `publish: true # why` and `publish: maybe` publish one, and `publish: "False"` is visible while `publish: FALSE` is not. The four keys are consulted in ONE order on every page the build copies — publishForSection<N>, publish, draftSection<N>, draft — so where a page LIVES decides only which key is WRITTEN: `sectionLocal` is carried on every case below and must not change the answer. Measured 2026-09-18 against python-frontmatter 1.3.0 / PyYAML 6.0.3 / js-yaml on JSON_SCHEMA, and re-measured on every `verify.sh` run by `scripts/check_visibility_against_the_site.py`; the table and what was rejected are in documentation/08-course-config-reference.md. DELIBERATELY NOT HERE: forms neither app should claim to read — a value on the line BELOW the key, a tag (`!!str false`), a block scalar, an anchor or alias, a flow collection, an escape inside double quotes, an indented key, and frontmatter the build cannot parse at all (tab indentation, an unclosed fence), which stops the whole build so there is no site verdict to mirror. Each app answers `cannot tell` internally for those and its REPORTING collapses that to visible — never to hidden, because calling a page hidden while students are reading it is the failure that reports success — while anything that WRITES refuses to trust it and writes the flag out in full. They are pinned in each platform's own tests rather than here, because a shared case saying `expectVisible: true` about a form the site HIDES would oblige the other platform to be wrong in the same direction. WITH ONE DELIBERATE EXCEPTION, added 2026-09-19 with issue #176: the last two cases below are `cannot tell` forms and ARE carried here, because for those two the site PUBLISHES the page and so does each app's reporting. The test is not "can the reader read it" but "does the reporting answer match the site" — where those two agree, a shared case obliges nobody to be wrong, and these two are worth carrying because the reader that got them wrong got them wrong CONFIDENTLY, which is what let a writer's already-right gate turn "hide this page" into a no-op.

readingCases.why: The plain case.
The other plain case.
The build loads every page with PyYAML, which is YAML 1.1: `yes` IS the boolean true, and the page arrives at Quartz as `publish: true`.
The one that surprises everybody. `no` is YAML 1.1's boolean false, so the page is HIDDEN — a reader that only knows `true`/`false` calls this page visible while students cannot see it.
`on` is the third spelling of true.
And `off` the third spelling of false.
All caps is one of the nine spellings PyYAML resolves.
So is this one, and the page is hidden.
Capitalised is a spelling too. Exactly three cases of each word are: all lower, Initial, ALL CAPS.
And nothing else is. `oN` is not one of the nine, so it stays the STRING "oN", and a string that is not "false" publishes the page.
Same rule, on the word that matters most: mixed case is an ordinary string, and the page is VISIBLE. A reader that lowercases before comparing hides a page the site publishes.
Anything PyYAML cannot make a boolean of becomes a string, and every string except "false" is published. Plantoir must not report this page held back.
A teacher may well type `y`, and PyYAML deliberately does NOT read a single letter as a boolean — so the page is published, whatever they meant.
The dangerous half of the same rule: `n` looks like `no` and does the opposite. The page is PUBLISHED.
A number is not a boolean here. Zero publishes the page.

Annotating a flag with a reason is an ordinary thing to do in Obsidian. The build strips the comment before Quartz sees the page, so it changes nothing — this is the case issue #140 was opened for, where Plantoir listed a live page as held back.
The comment changes nothing in this direction either.
A `#` with no space in front of it does not start a comment. The value is the string "false#x", which is not "false", so the page is PUBLISHED.
Quotes stop PyYAML resolving the word, so Quartz gets the string "false" — and `patches/publish.ts` holds a page back for that string as well as for the boolean.

And THIS page is visible, one capital letter away from the one above. The quotes keep it a string, and the string comparison in `patches/publish.ts` is exact: "False" is not "false". Do not "simplify" this into a case-insensitive check — it would hide a page the site publishes.
Quoting cuts the other way too: quoted, `no` never becomes the boolean, so this page is published where the unquoted spelling hides it.
A quoted "true" is a string, and every string but "false" is published.
A key with nothing after it is null, and null is not false. The page is published.
YAML's own spelling of null. Same answer.
And the word. Same answer again.
Both rules at once: the comment goes, and `Off` is the boolean false.
A page carrying the same key twice: the LAST one wins, because that is what PyYAML keeps. A reader that stops at the first line reports the opposite of what students see.
The same rule pointing the other way, so neither answer can be right by accident.
A space before the colon is still the key `publish`. YAML allows it and the page is hidden.
A quoted KEY is the same key. The page is hidden.
The legacy key means the opposite. Reading it as-is publishes a page the teacher hid.
And the other way round.
The build asks `build_site._as_bool`, which takes a real boolean as itself — so an unquoted `yes` is true, and the page is held back.
`on` is a boolean true as well, so this page is held back too.

Mixed case is a STRING here, and `_as_bool` lowercases a string before comparing it with "true". So this page IS held back — the opposite of what mixed case does on the `publish:` side, and the reason the two families need two predicates.
Quoted, so it never becomes a boolean, and "yes" lowercased is not "true". This page is PUBLISHED where the unquoted spelling two cases up hides it.
And a quoted "true" still holds the page back, because that is the one string `_as_bool` compares against.
Anything that is neither a boolean true nor the text "true" leaves the page published.
A number is not true here, whatever a teacher meant by it.
The comment is gone before the value is read, on this key as on the other.
A course-level page carries one flag per section.
And the same key can hold it back.
The per-section legacy spelling, inverted like its plain counterpart.
The legacy key with a YAML 1.1 spelling of true: the build hides this page. Anything that carries this page's visibility to another section must invert THIS, not the literal text "true".
A key naming ANOTHER section says nothing about this one — the build deletes it unread. Section 1 sees a page with no flag, which is visible.

A plain `publish:` on a COURSE-LEVEL page still counts: the build consults all four keys on every page it copies, wherever the page lives. Until 2026-09-18 the mac read only the per-section keys here and reported this page visible while the build hid it.
Precedence, first pair: `publishForSection<N>` wins over a plain `publish`.
Precedence, second pair: a `publish` of either spelling wins over the legacy key. A page carrying both has already been migrated, and the leftover must not contradict it.
Precedence, third pair: between the two legacy spellings the per-section one wins. The whole order is publishForSection<N>, publish, draftSection<N>, draft.
`sectionLocal` is true here and the per-section key is still the one that answers: where a page LIVES decides which key is WRITTEN, and nothing about how it is read.
The same point from the other side: `sectionLocal` is false and a plain `publish` still answers.

No space after the colon, so this is not a mapping at all — it is one plain scalar, and the page reaches Quartz with NO keys and is PUBLISHED. Measured. A reader that takes everything after the first colon calls this page hidden while students are reading it, which is the one mistake that must never be made. (With another key beside it the same line stops the build instead, so there is no case here for that shape.)
The same rule with the value that makes it look harmless: `publish:true` is not this page's flag either. Both spellings are here so neither answer can be right by accident.
A page that says nothing is VISIBLE — that is Quartz's own default, and changing it here would hide every page written before the field existed.

A value CONTINUES onto the next line whenever the line below is indented, however complete the key's own line looks: YAML folds the two into the one plain scalar "false false", a STRING that is not "false", and the page is PUBLISHED. Measured 2026-09-19, python-frontmatter 1.3.0 / PyYAML 6.0.3. Both readers answer `cannot tell` here and their reporting collapses that to visible, which is what the site does — so this case is honest as a shared one, unlike the other continuation forms, whose reporting answer is visible where the site HIDES. The reason it matters is the WRITER: reading the key's line alone called this page hidden CONFIDENTLY, so the already-right gate made "hide this page" a no-op while students could read it.

The same rule with a BLANK LINE in between, which is the row a reader that looked only at the next physical line would miss. Measured 2026-09-19: the fold is "false\nfalse", still a string that is not "false", and the page is PUBLISHED. Honest as a shared case for the same reason as the row above — both readers step over the blank before they test the indent, answer `cannot tell`, and report visible, which is what the site does. The polarity siblings (`no`, `off`, `FALSE`, `true`, `maybe` with a value below) are equally honest and add no coverage these two do not; they stay in each platform's own tests.

writingCases.note: The runnable half of `writingRules` above — give `before` to the writer, ask it for `setVisible`, and expect `after` and `expectChanged` exactly. `before` and `after` are WHOLE files, newline for newline, not the frontmatter fragments `readingCases` uses. Deliberately inside the subset both apps handle identically: LF endings, no inline `# comment` after a value being REWRITTEN (both platforms build a migrated line fresh and so drop one; where they differ is rewriting a key that is already current, which Windows' `ReplaceValue` preserves and the mac's line rewrite does not), no indented keys, and no blank line before the opening fence. A value's CONTINUATION lines are inside that subset as of 2026-09-19 (issue #176) and the last three cases cover them: for a key line with no inline comment and no leading indent, the mac's whole-line rebuild and Windows' `ReplaceValue` produce the same bytes, and both sweep with the same walk. Two continuation forms are still kept OUT for the usual reason — a column-0 `# note` between a key and its value, and a column-0 block sequence under an empty key, where the two agree today but the reasoning is odd enough to carry better in each platform's own test. What a NON-BOOLEAN value means is no longer deferred as 'a reader question': `readingCases` settles it, and the last three cases below say what the writer must then do with the answer — leave a page alone when it already SAYS what was asked, however oddly it says it, and write the flag out in full when the reading was `cannot tell`. A writer must never collapse `cannot tell` the way reporting does; erring visible is a mild mistake in a sentence and a page published behind the teacher's back in a file. BOTH suites run this list as of 2026-09-19: the mac since 2026-09-09 (issue #107), and Windows since issue #138, which replaced five of these cases retyped into its own test file. Three of the other five were already asserted there in that suite's own words; what the loop adds is that every case is read from the FILE and so cannot drift from it (ten on the day; thirteen since #176), and that cases 7 and 9 — a block carrying neither spelling, and an oddly-worded `published` asked to be HIDDEN — are covered there for the first time. Said here, and dated, because this note claimed the opposite for a day — a false statement about which side runs a list is how a gap survives review.

writingRules.detail: Publishing a `draftSection1: true` page writes `publishForSection1: true` on the SAME line, and the `draftSection1` line is gone; a page carrying BOTH spellings loses the legacy one. The new key takes the old key's position, so a migrated page shows a one-line diff in Obsidian rather than reordered frontmatter.
writingRules.rule: A page written in the old spelling is MIGRATED to the new key, and the legacy key removed, the first time something edits its visibility
writingRules.why: Decided 2026-09-07 (Russell), replacing the rule this list carried since it was written — 'a page written in the old spelling KEEPS it, inverted' — which the mac implemented and Windows never did. Migration leaves a teacher's file in one current spelling rather than two competing ones, stops the old key accumulating forever, and is what documentation/04-course-setup.md and 08-course-config-reference.md have described all along. There is no flag day: the build reads both spellings, so a legacy course builds exactly as before and converts one page at a time. Rejected: keeping the old key inverted (the mac's behaviour until 2026-09-09, when it adopted this — issue #107) — it would make both documentation files wrong and leave teachers' pages carrying a legacy key indefinitely; and leaving the divergence recorded but unresolved, which is how a knownDivergence becomes permanent.
writingRules.migrationIsTheOneExceptionToRule4: A legacy page whose value is already right is still rewritten, once, to migrate the key — although 'writing the value it already has changes nothing' says a no-op write must not touch the file. Deliberate, and it is a property of the WRITER rather than of any plan: both plan layers drop a page whose visibility already matches into their 'already right' list and never write it, so no plan asks for this write. One thing does — the mac's copy-a-class tool sets the new page hidden from the SOURCE page's frontmatter with no such filter, so a copy of a legacy hidden page is born migrated. (The third writer, the re-date overflow, is gated on the page being visible, so it cannot reach it either — said here so the next reader does not re-derive it.) It is pinned for that one and for the day something else does — a sweep, a repair, a tool that sets rather than toggles — the cost is one page's modification time moving once, and it buys a course that converges on one spelling instead of carrying legacy keys on exactly the pages nobody ever flips. A rule that migrated only on a genuine change would leave those pages old forever. (This sentence said 'reachable only inside a batch that is changing OTHER pages' until 2026-09-09, when implementing it on the mac showed that a batch skips such a page too — corrected rather than deleted, so nobody goes looking again for the code path it described.)

writingRules.rule: Edit the LINE, never round-trip the YAML
writingRules.why: A YAML library reorders keys and strips comments. The frontmatter is the teacher's, and they will see the diff in Obsidian.

writingRules.detail: Report 'no change' rather than rewriting the file. One exception, on purpose: a legacy-spelled page is migrated even when its value is already right — see the first rule.
writingRules.rule: Writing the value it already has changes nothing
writingRules.why: A no-op write still updates the modification time, which makes the next build think the content changed.

It is redundant with the file's own name, which is why nothing broke: the mac reads it with the filename's section as the fallback, and Windows does not read it at all. Keep writing it — a timetable copied out of its folder, or attached to a problem report, still says what it is for.
Plain dates, not a recurrence rule. A school timetable has holidays, PA days and the week the schedule turned inside out for exams — no rule survives contact with it.

Where the dates came from, IN THE TEACHER'S OWN WORDS — 'timetable.xlsx, block H'. It is what they read months later when they wonder where these came from, and 'a Google Sheet' answers that far less well than they can themselves. Read back as 'not recorded' when absent rather than blank.
When they were written down, so a teacher can tell a timetable from last semester.

sidebarHiding.note: What the entries of course_config.json's `hidden` list MEAN, and who may change them. Issue #265: the switches under 'Hide from the site's sidebar' in Course Settings did not always match the built sidebar.

matchRule.rule: `hidden` holds the STORED names of TOP-LEVEL items of the built site: a file by its file name with `.md` ("Key Links.md"), a folder by its folder name ("Tasks"). An entry hides the top-level item of that name and everything inside it, matched ignoring case and Unicode normalisation. Nothing below the top level is hidden by a name. A name without `.md` also hides the top-level file `<name>.md`.
matchRule.why: Version 1 of the site's filter matched a file on its page TITLE and a folder on its name at ANY depth, and the build stripped `.md` so a file name could stand in for a title. Course Settings offers and writes FILE names of TOP-LEVEL items, so a page whose title was not its file name was never hidden (measured: 'Learning Goals.md' titled 'Goals for Learning' stayed in the sidebar), and a nested folder or page sharing a ticked name was hidden by accident. Case and normalisation are ignored because the Mac's disk ignores them: 'tasks' typed for the folder 'Tasks', or a name stored composed while the disk has it decomposed, is the same folder, and this errs toward hiding. The name-without-.md alias keeps every older entry hiding what it hid. Measured to change nothing on Russell's 7 real courses, all 38 example payloads and all 50 skeletons. The one direction toward SHOWING is a nested item sharing a ticked name, which the switch list never offered.
matchRule.consumers: scripts/check_sidebar_hiding_against_the_site.py runs every case through the REAL Quartz file tree and the filter text the build writes (verify.sh, in the image). scripts/test_sidebar_hiding.py checks the cases are well formed. Each built section's copy of the filter is brought up to date by build_site.ensure_sidebar_hide_rule_current.

buildKeepsHidden.rule: A build's preflight never changes `hidden`. A folder it discovers (on disk, not yet in its scope's list) is still added to shared_folders or per_section_folders and to expandable, but if its name is already in `hidden` it STAYS hidden.
buildKeepsHidden.why: The build used to un-hide such a folder and write the list back ('Un-hid newly discovered folder'). A folder ticked hidden and then moved to the other level, made again at the other level, or listed in the wrong scope was un-hidden on EVERY build, the tick erased from the file while Course Settings still showed it, and the next Save put it back - measured on all five shapes below with the real preflight. Keeping it hidden errs the safe way: hiding from the sidebar never unpublishes a page. Rejected: limiting the un-hide to names the teacher could not have ticked - the Settings form offers only names already listed, so every name in `hidden` was ticked by somebody, or is a legacy entry nobody should lose silently.

workLease.note: A work lease: a file saying which process is doing what, so other windows, other copies of Plantoir and outside assistants leave that work alone. Windows' WorkLease (Plantoir.Core/Assist/WorkLease.cs) set the shape; the mac matches it and adds a fourth line. The rules a reader applies are shared-rules.json -> workLeases. #245 wrote this block for the import's lease; #156 adds the kinds it writes (build, preview, publish) and any name cases here rather than a second block.
workLease.directory: courses/.internal/activity/ inside the working folder. Written outside the thing it is about on purpose: removing a staging folder must not remove the claim to it.
workLease.name: <NAME>.<kind>.<pid>.lease - NAME is the course code for build, preview, publish and assist, and the FOLDER name being made for import; kind is one word; pid is the owner's process id in decimal. Read from the END (the pid is the second-last dot-separated part, the kind the third-last), because a folder name may itself contain dots.

kinds.import: A reference course's staging folder is being made (the mac's import and Keep a Copy for Reference...). Written by the mac since #206; four lines since #245. Held for the whole making of the folder, released when it is renamed into place or tidied away.
kinds.build: Written by Windows today; the mac from #156.
kinds.preview: Written by Windows today; the mac from #156.
kinds.publish: Written by Windows today; the mac from #156.
kinds.assist: Written by Windows' plantoir-mcp when started with a course lock.

lines: 2: the owner's process name as the system reports it - Plantoir for the app, its MCP server and a scheduled run, which are one program. The mac writes ProcessInfo.processName as of #245; #156 makes it the process table's own name (sysctl p_comm), because processName is argv[0]'s last part and differs through a symlink (measured: a lease written that way read its own live writer as gone).

3: the moment the lease was taken, UTC, in .NET's round-trip 'O' form - 2026-09-25T13:59:23.8960000Z (seven fractional digits). No reader parses it; it is there for parity and for a person reading the folder.

4: (mac only) when the owner STARTED, as whole seconds since 1970, a dot, and the microseconds padded to six digits - 1790345209.217862 - read from the process table. Windows' reader reads lines 1 and 2 and ignores this one.
workLease.encoding: UTF-8, no byte-order mark, each line ending in a line feed, the last included. A reader accepts carriage returns before the line feeds. The mac writes atomically (a reader never meets half a file).
workLease.olderShapes: The mac's import wrote ONE line - the process id - from #206 until #245, and an older copy of Plantoir still does. A reader judges such a lease as written by Plantoir - the only program that ever wrote one - rather than ignoring it, because ignoring it would sweep an older copy's live import, and rather than on the id alone, because after a restart the id of a crashed one can belong to an unrelated process for the whole uptime (shared-rules.json -> workLeases.liveness, the two 'import' cases). Windows' own reader treats fewer than two lines as stale; it does not read import leases today.
